signals.title: @OwenGregorian: AI Weapons That Can Choose Who to Kill Are Already Here. The UN Warns the World is Crossing a Dangerous Line | Rupendra Brahambhatt, ZME Sci
signals.content: AI Weapons That Can Choose Who to Kill Are Already Here. The UN Warns the World is Crossing a Dangerous Line | Rupendra Brahambhatt, ZME Science According to the United Nations (UN) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), AI-powered weapons are now being developed with the ability to identify targets and, in some cases, make the final decision to attack without waiting for a human command. “Autonomous weapons systems are not part of a distant future — a race toward greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway,” the UN and ICRC representatives said in a joint statement. The battlefield is making the debate less hypothetical The technology that enables an AI-enhanced weapon, such as a quadcopter drone rigged with explosives, to target humans without any human supervision is not widely deployed, but according to some reports, it has already been used on the battlefield. In July, a Russian Molniya drone reportedly killed three civilians in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia city after being launched toward an area near a gas station. Forensic investigations reveal the drone appears to have used onboard AI to select its final target rather than relying on a human operator. Although the exact drone involved in the civilian deaths was not recovered, investigators examining similar drones found Nvidia Jetson Orin computers, no apparent antenna for human control, and software containing predefined target categories. “The weapons had no antenna for human piloting and had a powerful onboard computer with pretrained target categories,” Stuart Russell, an expert in computer science and the president of the International Association for Safe & Ethical AI, told The Los Angeles Times. To be clear, military automation has existed for decades. What is changing is the possibility of removing humans from the final part of the “kill chain” altogether. The real fight is over what human control means The more we give AI the freedom of making decisions on its own, the more critical it becomes to understand how much human involvement is necessary, especially in a battlefield setting where the risk to non-combatants is very real. One approach, long discussed internationally, is “meaningful human control” — the idea that people should retain meaningful involvement in decisions to use lethal force. However, governments and industry experts have struggled to agree on what that actually requires. “The concept of Meaningful Human Control (MHC) has been bantered about over the last ten years, and in this back and forth, it has been fundamentally misunderstood and misrepresented, largely by the same sets of actors (academics, political leaders, and civil society) for a variety of reasons,” said Heather M. Roff, an expert on AI and autonomous weapon systems and a senior research scientist at the Center for Naval Analyses. The United States government has increasingly used the phrase ‘appropriate human judgment,’ which refers to human oversight across the weapon’s design, testing, deployment and rules of engagement rather than requiring a person to approve every individual strike. Under that approach, a weapon could potentially make the targeting decision itself, as long as humans had exercised judgment at other stages — such as deciding where, when and under what conditions the system could be used. This is where the debate gets complicated: does human oversight earlier in the process count if a machine ultimately chooses the target? Moreover, the problem is becoming harder to contain. AI-powered weapon systems are getting more capable and cheaper, making them increasingly attractive for warfare. Once a weapon demonstrates a battlefield advantage, giving it up becomes politically and militarily much harder to do. Why the UN and Red Cross are pushing now The UN and ICRC first called for specific restrictions on autonomous weapons three years ago. They have now renewed that appeal with greater urgency, warning that weapons technology is advancing faster than international rules governing it. Their position is not simply a call to ban every autonomous weapon. They want clear prohibitions and restrictions, particularly on weapons that can autonomously target humans and systems whose effects cannot be reliably predicted. This is very important because an autonomous system attacking an incoming missile is fundamentally different from one deciding which person to kill. “We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: The autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” the UN Secretary-General and ICRC head said. The organizations also warn about accountability. If a machine independently selects a target, responsibility can become harder to trace when civilians are killed. Does it lie with the programmer, manufacturer, commander, operator or state? Meanwhile, autonomous weapons are being developed against the backdrop of wars in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan and elsewhere. Scientists and engineers working on military AI have also raised concerns about where the technology is heading. The UN and ICRC argue that waiting until such weapons become commonplace could make meaningful restrictions impossible to enforce. https://t.co/tyxljqmlH0

signals.content: MizarVision | CHINA A Chinese geospatial intelligence company says it has developed its own AI-powered big-data model capable of fusing multiple sensor streams, including commercial satellite imagery and open-source data. According to the company’s Weibo post, the system is designed to combine multisource remote-sensing and sensor data to deliver faster and more accurate real-world intelligence. The statement highlights a broader trend in China’s GEOINT sector: moving beyond raw satellite imagery toward AI-assisted sensor fusion, automated analysis and near-real-time intelligence products. The key development is not simply access to satellite data, but the ability to integrate different sources into a single analytical environment — potentially accelerating detection, classification and assessment of events on the ground. MizarVision will continue monitoring developments in Chinese commercial satellite intelligence and AI-enabled GEOINT. #China #GEOINT #OSINT #SatelliteIntelligence
